HX-400 Centrifugal Process Pump
Installation, Operation and Maintenance Manual
Document number | HX-IOM-400-EN-R7
Revision | R7
Issue date | 2026-03-18
Applies to | HX-400/A, HX-400/S, HX-400/D, all build numbers from 400-0412 onward
Supersedes | HX-IOM-400-EN-R6 of 2024-06-02
Issued by | Halstrom Pompen B.V., Zwolle, Nederland
Language | English (original). Dutch translation available as HX-IOM-400-NL-R7.
Read this manual before installing, operating or servicing the pump. Keep it with the machine for the whole of its service life. If the pump is sold on, this manual goes with it.
The information in this manual applies to the pump as delivered. Halstrom accepts no liability for damage arising from modifications carried out without written approval, from the use of non-original parts, or from operation outside the limits stated in section 12.

0.1 How to use this manual
Sections 1 to 4 cover safety, delivery and what the machine is. Sections 5 to 7 take the pump from the crate to its first running hour. Sections 8 and 9 are for the people who run and service it day to day. Section 10 is the fault-finding table, section 11 the strip-down and rebuild, and section 12 holds the numbers.
Three kinds of notice appear in the text:
DANGER An instruction that, if ignored, will cause death or serious injury.
CAUTION An instruction that, if ignored, may damage the pump or the installation.
A note gives background or a practical hint. It carries no safety weight.

0.2 Contents
1 Safety 2 Transport and storage 3 Receiving inspection 4 Description of the pump 5 Installation 6 Electrical connection 7 Commissioning 8 Operation 9 Maintenance 10 Fault finding 11 Dismantling and reassembly 12 Technical data 13 Spare parts 14 Appendices Page numbers are not printed in the contents of this revision; use the section numbers in the page header.

1 Safety
1.1 Intended use
The HX-400 is a single-stage, end-suction centrifugal pump for clean and lightly contaminated liquids. It is designed for continuous duty in industrial process service: cooling water, condensate, process water, light hydrocarbons and, in the duplex variant, chloride-bearing media.
The pump is not suitable for liquids containing abrasive solids above 50 mg/l, for slurries, for media that gas off inside the casing, or for service above the temperature limits in section 12.2. Using it outside these limits voids the warranty and may cause the seal to fail without warning.
DANGER Never run the pump against a closed discharge valve for longer than 60 seconds. The liquid in the casing heats rapidly and the casing may rupture. The temperature rise at zero flow is about 9 kelvin per minute for the HX-400.

[1 Safety]
1.2 Qualification of personnel
Installation, commissioning and maintenance may be carried out only by people who are trained for the work and who have read this manual. Electrical work is reserved for qualified electricians. Work on pumps that have carried hazardous media additionally requires the permit described in the operator's own procedure.
Activity | Minimum qualification | Permit required
Visual inspection, reading instruments | Operator, instructed | No
Topping up oil, greasing | Mechanical technician | No
Oil change, filter change | Mechanical technician | No
Alignment, coupling work | Mechanical technician, alignment trained | Isolation permit
Seal replacement | Mechanical fitter | Isolation permit
Bearing replacement, rotor work | Mechanical fitter, workshop | Isolation permit
Opening the casing on hazardous service | Mechanical fitter | Isolation permit and, where entry is needed, a confined space entry permit

[1 Safety > 1.2 Qualification of personnel]
Activity | Minimum qualification | Permit required
Electrical connection, motor work | Qualified electrician | Electrical isolation permit
Table 1.1 - Who may do what. The permits named are those of the operating company; Halstrom does not issue permits.
1.3 Residual risks
Even when the pump is installed and operated correctly, the following risks remain and must be managed by the operating company:
• Hot surfaces. The casing and the bearing housing reach the temperature of the pumped liquid. Above 60 C the surfaces must be guarded or marked.
• Rotating parts. The coupling guard must be in place before the motor is energised. The guard is part of the CE conformity of the unit.
• Stored pressure. The casing holds pressure after the pump stops. Vent through the casing vent before loosening any joint.
• Residual liquid. The casing drains incompletely; about 4 litres remain in the volute of an HX-400 after the drain plug is opened.

[1 Safety > 1.3 Residual risks]
• Noise. Sound pressure at one metre is 78 dB(A) at the duty point and rises toward the end of the curve. Hearing protection is required above 80 dB(A).
• Electrostatic charge. When pumping non-conductive liquids the casing must be bonded to the plant earth.

[1 Safety]
1.5 Modifications and spare parts
Any modification to the pressure-containing parts, to the shaft or to the sealing arrangement requires written approval from Halstrom. Welding on the casing is not permitted in the field under any circumstances; a cracked casing is replaced, not repaired.
Only original spare parts carry the material certification the pressure equipment conformity depends on. Where a non-original part is fitted, the operating company becomes the manufacturer of the modified assembly in the sense of the Machinery Directive.

2 Transport and storage
2.1 Lifting
The bare pump weighs 410 kg; the pump on its baseplate with motor weighs between 980 and 1140 kg depending on the motor frame. The weight is stamped on the nameplate and on the shipping crate.
DANGER Lift the assembled unit by the four baseplate lifting points only. Lifting by the pump eyebolt alone will tip the unit: the eyebolt is rated for the bare pump. Never lift by the motor eyebolt when the motor is bolted to the baseplate.

2.2 Storage before installation
Pumps are shipped with the casing drained, the internals preserved and the flanges blanked. The preservation is good for twelve months in a dry indoor store at between 5 and 40 C with relative humidity below 70%.
Storage period | Required action | Interval
Up to 3 months | No action beyond keeping the blanks in place. | -
3 to 12 months | Rotate the shaft by hand six full turns. | Monthly
3 to 12 months | Check the desiccant bag in the bearing housing. | Quarterly
Over 12 months | Renew the internal preservation; replace the bearing grease before commissioning. | Annually
Over 24 months | Return to the workshop for inspection. Seals are replaced as a matter of course. | -
Outdoor storage | Not permitted for longer than 14 days, and only under a weatherproof cover with the drains open. | -

section: 2 Transport and storage > 2.2 Storage before installation
text:
[2 Transport and storage > 2.2 Storage before installation]
The elastomeric coupling element ages whether the pump runs or not. An element that has been in store for more than four years is replaced on commissioning regardless of its appearance.
2.3 Unpacking
Remove the flange blanks only when the pipework is ready to be connected. Foreign objects left in the casing are the single most common cause of damage during the first start: a blanking plate, a rag or a welding rod will destroy the impeller in seconds.

4 Description of the pump

[4 Description of the pump]
4.2 Construction
The HX-400 is a back pull-out design. The bearing housing, shaft, impeller and seal come out of the casing as one assembly once the coupling spacer and the casing bolts are removed; the casing stays bolted to the pipework. This is the reason the casing bolt torque in section 5.7 matters so much: those bolts are disturbed at every overhaul.
The rotor runs in two bearings. The drive end carries a 6309 C3 deep groove ball bearing taking radial load; the non-drive end carries a 3309 C3 double row angular contact bearing taking the hydraulic axial thrust. Both are oil lubricated from the common sump in the bearing housing.
Axial thrust is balanced by back vanes on the impeller shroud rather than by balance holes. Back vanes also keep solids out of the seal chamber, which is why the seal faces last longer on this design than on the superseded HX-380.

[4 Description of the pump]
4.3 Sealing arrangement
The standard arrangement is a MS-28 single-acting cartridge seal, part number HX-4-SEAL-28S. The seal is supplied as a complete cartridge with setting clips; it is not rebuilt in the field. Expected life in clean water service at 40 C is 16,000 operating hours.

4.5 Wear rings and clearances
Pump efficiency falls as the wear ring clearance opens up. The clearance is measured at every overhaul and the rings are renewed when the measured value reaches the scrap figure.
Dimension | New (mm) | Acceptable (mm) | Scrap at (mm)
Casing ring to impeller ring, diametral | 0.45 - 0.55 | up to 0.90 | 0.95
Throat bush to sleeve, diametral | 0.35 - 0.45 | up to 0.70 | 0.75
Impeller front face to casing, axial | 1.8 - 2.2 | 1.5 - 2.6 | below 1.3
Shaft runout at seal, TIR | max 0.03 | max 0.05 | 0.06
Shaft runout at coupling, TIR | max 0.04 | max 0.06 | 0.08
Bearing housing bore, drive end | 100.000 - 100.022 | to 100.040 | 100.045
Table 4.4 - Clearances. A diametral clearance of 0.95 mm costs roughly four efficiency points at the duty point.

5 Installation
5.1 Location
Allow 800 mm clear in front of the bearing housing for back pull-out, and 600 mm above the unit for lifting. A pump that cannot be pulled out without dismantling pipework will not be maintained properly, whatever the maintenance schedule says.
The foundation must be able to carry three times the static weight of the unit and must be isolated from the building structure where vibration transmission matters.

[5 Installation]
5.2 Foundation and grouting
Set the baseplate on levelling screws or shim packs at the foundation bolt positions, level it in both directions to within 0.2 mm per metre, and grout with a non-shrink cementitious grout. Do not tighten the foundation bolts to their final torque until the grout has cured for the time the grout manufacturer states, typically seven days.
Step | Action | Tolerance or value
1 | Clean and roughen the foundation surface | Remove all laitance
2 | Place the baseplate on levelling screws | Four corners plus centre
3 | Level across the pump pedestal | 0.2 mm/m
4 | Level along the baseplate | 0.2 mm/m
5 | Check the coupling gap roughly | 4 mm nominal
6 | Pour grout, vent all pockets | Non-shrink, 60 MPa
7 | Cure | Per grout data sheet, typically 7 days
8 | Remove levelling screws, fill the pockets | -
9 | Torque foundation bolts M24 | 650 Nm lubricated
10 | Re-check level after bolting | 0.2 mm/m
11 | Record on the installation sheet | Appendix B

[5 Installation > 5.2 Foundation and grouting]
Table 5.1 - Foundation sequence.
5.3 Pipework
Pipework must be supported independently of the pump. The forces and moments the flanges can carry are given in section 12.5; they are small, and exceeding them pulls the casing out of round, which shows up as a seal that keeps failing for no apparent reason.
• Suction line as short and as straight as possible. Allow at least five pipe diameters of straight pipe before the suction flange.
• No high points in the suction line that can trap air. Where the line must rise, fit a vent.
• Eccentric reducer on the suction, flat side up, to avoid an air pocket.
• Isolating valve in both suction and discharge, and a non-return valve in the discharge between the pump and the isolating valve.
• Strainer in the suction line during commissioning, removed after the first 100 operating hours unless the service requires it permanently.

[5 Installation > 5.3 Pipework]
• Pressure gauge connections on both suction and discharge within two pipe diameters of the flanges.
CAUTION Never use the pump as an anchor point to pull pipework into line. Flange faces must meet without being forced: a gap of more than 1.5 mm or a lateral offset of more than 1.0 mm before bolting means the pipework has to be corrected first.

[5 Installation]
5.4 Flange gaskets
Service | Gasket | Thickness | Seating stress
Water to 100 C | Graphite laminate with tanged insert | 2.0 mm | 30 MPa
Water 100 - 140 C | Graphite laminate with tanged insert | 2.0 mm | 35 MPa
Light hydrocarbons | Spiral wound 316/graphite | 4.5 mm | 70 MPa
Chloride-bearing | PTFE enveloped with graphite core | 3.0 mm | 25 MPa
Thermal oil | Spiral wound 316/graphite | 4.5 mm | 70 MPa
Table 5.2 - Gasket selection by service.
A gasket is a single-use item. Re-using a graphite laminate gasket is the second most common cause of a flange leak after incorrect bolt torque.

[5 Installation]
5.5 Flange bolting - general
Flange joints are tightened in a crosswise pattern in at least three passes: 30% of final torque, 70%, then 100%. A fourth pass at 100% in a clockwise sequence confirms that no bolt has relaxed. Re-check the torque after the first thermal cycle and again after 24 hours of operation on services above 100 C.
All torque figures in this manual are for lubricated threads and bolt faces, using a molybdenum disulphide paste or an equivalent anti-seize with a friction coefficient of 0.12. If the threads are dry, multiply the figure by 1.3. Using the lubricated figure on dry threads leaves the joint under-stressed; using the dry figure on lubricated threads over-stresses the bolt and may yield it.

DANGER The impeller nut has a LEFT-HAND thread. It is slackened clockwise and tightened anti-clockwise. Fitters who have not worked on this frame before routinely shear the shaft end by applying increasing torque in the wrong direction.
5.8 Alignment
Align the coupling after the grout has cured, after the pipework is connected and bolted, and again after the first thermal cycle. Alignment before the pipework is connected proves nothing: the act of bolting a badly fitted pipe to the flange moves the pump.
Measurement | Cold limit | Hot check limit | Method

[5 Installation > 5.8 Alignment]
Measurement | Cold limit | Hot check limit | Method

Thermal growth on hot service shifts the pump upward relative to the motor. For water at 120 C the pump centreline rises about 0.09 mm; the cold alignment is offset downward by that amount so that the unit comes into line when hot.

6 Electrical connection
Electrical work is reserved for qualified electricians and is carried out under the operating company's electrical isolation procedure. The notes below concern only the interface with the pump.
6.1 Direction of rotation
CAUTION Check the direction of rotation with the coupling spacer removed. Running an HX-400 backwards for even a few seconds can unscrew the impeller nut, after which the impeller runs free inside the casing. Correct rotation is clockwise seen from the motor end, marked by an arrow cast into the bearing housing.

[6 Electrical connection]
6.3 Starting frequency
The motor may be started at most 6 times per hour, evenly spaced. More frequent starting overheats the rotor cage. Where process demand calls for more, fit a variable speed drive or a recirculation line rather than cycling the motor.

[7 Commissioning]
7.2 Priming
The pump is not self-priming. It must be filled with liquid and vented before every start after the casing has been opened or drained. On a flooded suction, open the suction valve and vent until liquid appears at the vent connection. On a suction lift, fill through the priming connection and vent.
DANGER Starting dry destroys the seal in under thirty seconds and can ignite flammable vapour through the heat generated at the seal faces. On flammable service the dry-running protection in table 6.1 is not optional.

section: 7 Commissioning > 7.3 First start and the first hour
text:
[7 Commissioning > 7.3 First start and the first hour]
The run-in oil change at 300 hours is the single most valuable maintenance action in the life of the pump. The oil drained at that point carries the running-in debris from the bearings and the gear faces; leaving it in place shortens bearing life measurably.

8 Operation
8.1 The operating window
The pump is designed to run near its best efficiency point. The further it runs from that point, the shorter the life of the seal and the bearings, whatever the maintenance regime.
Region | Flow as % of BEP | Allowed | Effect
Below minimum | under 15 | No | Recirculation, rapid temperature rise, seal failure
Minimum continuous | 15 - 50 | Yes, continuous | Raised radial load, shortened bearing life
Preferred | 70 - 115 | Yes, continuous | Design condition
High flow | 115 - 130 | Yes, intermittent | Rising NPSH requirement, cavitation risk
Run-out | over 130 | No | Motor overload, cavitation
Table 8.1 - Operating window referred to the best efficiency point. For an HX-400 at 2900 rpm with a 385 mm trim, BEP flow is 240 m3/h.

[8 Operation]
8.2 Routine observations
An operator walking the plant can detect most developing faults without instruments. The following are recorded once per shift on the log sheet in appendix D.
Observation | Normal | Act when
Suction pressure | Per the process | Falls by more than 0.3 bar from the usual value
Discharge pressure | Per the process | Falls by more than 5% at the same flow
Oil level | Centre of the sight glass | Below the lower mark or above the upper mark
Oil appearance | Clear amber | Milky (water ingress) or dark (overheating)
Seal | Dry or a drop every few minutes | Steady drip or any spray
Bearing housing temperature | Ambient plus 25 to 40 K | Above 80 C, or a rise of 10 K from the usual value
Noise | Steady hum | Gravel-like rattle (cavitation) or a periodic knock
Vibration | Below 4.5 mm/s | Above 4.5 mm/s, or any step change
Coupling guard | In place and secure | Loose or removed
Baseplate | Dry | Pooled liquid, loosened grout

[8 Operation > 8.2 Routine observations]
Table 8.2 - What the operator looks at each shift.
8.3 Minimum flow and recirculation
Minimum continuous flow for the HX-400 is 15 per cent of the best efficiency flow, that is 36 m3/h at the 385 mm trim. Below this figure the liquid recirculates inside the impeller eye, which raises the temperature in the casing and loads the bearings unevenly. Revision R5 of this manual raised the figure from 10 per cent after repeated recirculation damage in the field.
Where the process can call for less than minimum flow, fit an automatic recirculation valve returning to the suction vessel, not to the suction line: returning hot liquid directly to the suction line reduces the available NPSH and causes cavitation.

[8 Operation]
8.4 Stopping
Situation | Procedure
Normal stop | Close the discharge valve to about 10%, stop the motor, then close the suction valve if the pump is to stand idle.
Standby pump | Leave suction and discharge valves open; the non-return valve holds the line. Rotate the shaft a quarter turn weekly.
Stop for maintenance | Stop, isolate electrically under the LOTO procedure, close and lock both valves, vent the casing, then drain.
Emergency stop | Press the local stop. Do not close valves first; the non-return valve prevents reverse flow.
Long shutdown (over a month) | Drain the casing, flush if the medium crystallises, preserve per section 2.2, rotate the shaft monthly.
Freezing conditions | Drain the casing completely. Residual liquid in the volute will crack a cast iron casing.
Table 8.3 - Stopping procedures.

[8 Operation > 8.4 Stopping]
DANGER Never drain the casing while it is under pressure or while the liquid is above 60 C. Vent first through the casing vent, let the contents cool, and stand clear of the drain line when the plug is removed.

9.4 Oil change
Change the oil every 4,000 operating hours or every 12 months, whichever comes first, and at the run-in change after the first 300 hours. Change it earlier if the oil goes milky, which means water is entering past the seal, or if the acid number reaches the condemning limit.
Step | Action | Note
1 | Run the pump until the oil is warm, then stop and isolate. | Warm oil carries the debris out with it
2 | Place a drip tray holding at least 2 litres. | -
3 | Remove the drain plug at the bottom of the housing. | G 3/4, 40 Nm on refitting
4 | Let it drain for at least ten minutes. | Rotate the shaft by hand to clear the bearings
5 | Inspect the drained oil. | Bright particles mean bearing damage - investigate
6 | Fit a new sealing washer and refit the drain plug. | Never re-use the washer

[9 Maintenance > 9.4 Oil change]
Step | Action | Note
7 | Fill through the breather with 0.90 litre of Halstrom HLP-46. | To the centre of the sight glass
8 | Wait five minutes and re-check the level. | The level falls as the bearings fill
9 | Record the change and the running hours. | Appendix D log sheet
10 | Dispose of the used oil as waste oil. | Per the operating company's waste procedure
Table 9.4 - Oil change procedure.
CAUTION Overfilling is as damaging as underfilling. Oil above the centre of the sight glass is churned by the bearing cage, which raises the housing temperature by 15 to 20 kelvin and oxidises the oil.

[9 Maintenance]
9.5 Greasing
The pump bearings are oil lubricated and are never greased. The motor bearings are grease lubricated with Halstrom LGHP-2 at 2,000 operating hour intervals, or per the motor manufacturer's plate where that differs.
CAUTION Pumping grease into the pump bearing housing through the breather, which has happened in the field, destroys the bearings. The pump bearing housing has no grease nipple; if you are looking for one, you are at the wrong machine.

[9 Maintenance]
9.6 Mechanical seal replacement
The MS-28 single-acting cartridge seal is a cartridge unit, replaced complete. The faces are not lapped in the field and the cartridge is not opened. Expected life is 16,000 hours in clean water at up to 60 C, falling to about 8 000 hours above 100 C.
Step | Action | Value
1 | Isolate, drain and vent per the LOTO procedure | -
2 | Remove the coupling guard and the coupling spacer | -
3 | Disconnect the seal flush piping | Cap the open ends
4 | Slacken the casing bolts crosswise | 8 x M20
5 | Withdraw the back pull-out assembly | 86 kg, use slings
6 | Release the gland nuts and withdraw the old cartridge | 4 x M12
7 | Clean the shaft sleeve and check its runout | Max 0.03 mm TIR
8 | Check the seal chamber bore for scoring | Replace if scored
9 | Slide the new cartridge on, clips still fitted | Lubricate the O-ring with the pumped liquid, never with grease
10 | Tighten the gland nuts evenly | 65 Nm, equal gap all round

[9 Maintenance > 9.6 Mechanical seal replacement]
Step | Action | Value
11 | Tighten the sleeve grub screws | 22 Nm
12 | Remove the setting clips and keep them with the machine record | Without this the seal will not move axially
13 | Refit the assembly into the casing with a new gasket | Casing bolts 210 Nm
14 | Reconnect the flush, refit the spacer and guard | -
15 | Vent, prime and run in | Light weeping for the first hour is normal
Table 9.5 - Seal replacement. Step 12 is the step most often missed; a seal left with its clips in place will fail within hours.

[9 Maintenance]
9.7 Coupling
The Rexlite R-90 coupling uses an elastomeric element that ages whether the machine runs or not. Replace it every two years, or sooner if the element shows cracking at the root of the lugs, permanent set, or rubber dust inside the guard. Rubber dust is the reliable early sign.

[9 Maintenance]
9.8 Condition monitoring
Vibration is measured quarterly at both bearing housings in three directions. The overall RMS velocity is trended; a spectrum is recorded so that a rise can be attributed.
Frequency | Likely cause | Action
1 x running speed | Unbalance | Check for deposits or erosion on the impeller; rebalance at overhaul
2 x running speed | Misalignment | Re-align; check for pipe strain
Vane pass (5 x running speed) | Hydraulic, close clearance to the cutwater | Check the operating point against table 8.1
Below 1 x (0.4 - 0.48 x) | Oil whirl in the bearing | Check oil grade and level; check the bearing clearance
Bearing defect frequencies | Bearing damage | Plan a bearing change; sample the oil
Broadband, high frequency | Cavitation | Check NPSH available, suction strainer, suction valve position
Random, step change | Loose part or foreign object | Stop and investigate before the next start

[9 Maintenance > 9.8 Condition monitoring]
Table 9.6 - Reading the vibration spectrum. Alarm at 4.5 mm/s, trip at 7.1 mm/s overall RMS.
9.9 Judging wear without opening the pump
Wear ring clearance can be inferred from performance. At a fixed speed and a fixed suction condition, a fall in developed head of more than five per cent at the same flow, with no change in the process, indicates the clearance has opened. Confirm with a power reading: internal recirculation past worn rings raises the power drawn for the same delivered flow.

[11 Dismantling and reassembly]
11.3 Reassembly
Reassembly is the reverse of dismantling, with the following points that are specific to this frame:
• Heat bearings to 110 C in an induction heater and slide them on. Never drive a bearing on, and never heat above 125 C.
• The angular contact pair at the non-drive end is fitted back to back. Fitted the wrong way round, the pump will run but the bearings fail within a few hundred hours.
• Fit a new shaft sleeve O-ring and lubricate it with the pumped liquid, not with grease. Mineral grease swells FKM.
• The impeller nut is tightened anti-clockwise to 120 Nm. Lock it with the tab washer; the tab washer is a single-use part.
• Set the axial position of the rotor before the casing goes back on: impeller front face to casing 1.8 to 2.2 mm, adjusted at the bearing housing shims.
• Fit a new casing gasket dry. Do not use jointing compound; it prevents the correct gasket stress from developing.

[11 Dismantling and reassembly > 11.3 Reassembly]
• Tighten the casing bolts crosswise in three passes to 210 Nm.
• Fill with 0.90 litre of Halstrom HLP-46 before turning the shaft under power.
• Re-align after the casing is bolted back to the pipework, not before.
After an overhaul, run the pump in as if it were new: the run-in oil change at 300 hours applies again.

16 Worked example: checking NPSH
Most seal and bearing failures that are blamed on the pump are caused by cavitation, and cavitation is an installation problem. The calculation below is worth doing before blaming the machine.
The example is an HX-400 with a 385 mm impeller at 2900 rpm, pumping water at 70 C from a vented tank. The tank level is 2.4 metres above the pump centreline. The suction line is 18 metres of DN 150 with three bends and an open gate valve.
Step | Quantity | Value | Note
1 | Atmospheric pressure at the tank surface | 10.33 m | Vented tank at sea level
2 | Static head above the pump | +2.40 m | Tank level minus pump centreline
3 | Vapour pressure of water at 70 C | -3.20 m | From steam tables, 31.2 kPa
4 | Friction loss in the suction line | -0.95 m | 18 m of DN 150 at 240 m3/h, plus fittings
5 | Entrance loss and strainer | -0.35 m | Clean strainer. A dirty strainer can double this
6 | NPSH available | 8.23 m | Sum of steps 1 to 5

[16 Worked example: checking NPSH]
Step | Quantity | Value | Note
7 | NPSH required at 240 m3/h | 4.10 m | From table 12.4
8 | Margin | 4.13 m | Available minus required
9 | Minimum margin | 1.00 m | Section 12.4. 1.5 m on hydrocarbon service
10 | Verdict | Acceptable | The margin is comfortable at the duty point
Table 16.1 - NPSH check at the duty point.
Now repeat the calculation at 130 per cent flow, which is where the pump runs when the control valve opens fully:
Quantity | At 100% flow | At 130% flow | Change
NPSH required | 4.10 m | 7.40 m | +3.30 m
Friction loss in the suction line | 0.95 m | 1.61 m | Rises with the square of flow
Strainer loss | 0.35 m | 0.59 m | Same
NPSH available | 8.23 m | 7.33 m | -0.90 m
Margin | 4.13 m | -0.07 m | Cavitating
Table 16.2 - The same installation at the end of the curve. The margin has gone negative: the pump cavitates whenever the control valve opens fully, which is what the operator hears as a gravel rattle.

[16 Worked example: checking NPSH]
Note that nothing is wrong with the pump. The fix is a flow limit in the control system, or a larger suction line, or a lower liquid temperature. Replacing the seal again will not help.

I Decommissioning
At the end of its service life the pump is drained, flushed and dismantled. Materials are separated: cast iron and steel to scrap metal, stainless and duplex separately because of their value, bronze separately, elastomers and the seal faces to industrial waste, and the remaining oil to waste oil. The nameplate is removed and destroyed so that the machine cannot be re-sold with its certification.

This register lists every hazardous substance held or used by Rendell Industrial Services. A substance that is not in this register may not be brought on site or used on a client site without the VGM coordinator's written approval.

1 Purpose and scope
This document does two things. Sections 1 to 5 set out how Rendell manages safety on the work we do: who is responsible for what, how a job is assessed before it starts, and what protective equipment is required. Sections 6 to 9 are the substance register: a condensed data sheet for each hazardous substance we hold.
The procedures here apply alongside the client's own rules. Where the two differ, the stricter rule applies. Where a client rule would require us to work less safely than this document, the work stops and the supervisor is called.

2 Roles and responsibilities
Role | Responsible for | Can stop the work
Managing director | Providing the means: equipment, training, time and competent people | Yes
VGM coordinator | This register, the training matrix, incident investigation, approval of new substances | Yes
Site supervisor | The task risk assessment, the permit interface with the client, toolbox talks | Yes
Technician / fitter | The last-minute risk assessment before each task, using the right equipment, reporting near misses | Yes
Any person on site | Their own safety and that of those around them | Yes
Table 2.1 - Everyone on the list can stop the work. Nobody at Rendell needs permission to stop a job they believe is unsafe, and nobody has ever been disciplined for doing so.

3 Assessing the job
3.1 Task risk assessment
A written task risk assessment is prepared by the site supervisor before any of the following: work on a system that has carried a hazardous substance, work at height above two metres, lifting over 500 kg, hot work, entry into a confined space, or any first-time job at a client site.

section: 3 Assessing the job > 3.2 Last-minute risk assessment
text:
[3 Assessing the job]
3.2 Last-minute risk assessment
Every technician carries out a last-minute risk assessment at the work face, immediately before starting, every time. It takes about a minute and runs through six questions. The card is in appendix A and is carried in the toolbox.
# | Question | If the answer is no
1 | Do I understand the task and the method? | Ask the supervisor before touching anything
2 | Is the equipment isolated, locked and proved dead or depressurised? | Stop. Go back to WP-114
3 | Do I have the right tools, in good condition? | Fetch the right tool. Do not improvise
4 | Am I wearing the protective equipment this task needs? | Fetch it
5 | Could my work harm anyone else nearby? | Barrier off, warn them, or wait
6 | If something goes wrong, do I know how to raise the alarm and where the escape route is? | Find out first
Table 3.1 - The six-question last-minute risk assessment.

4 Personal protective equipment
4.1 Baseline
Safety shoes (S3), long trousers and long sleeves, and safety glasses are worn at all times in the workshop and on client sites. A helmet is worn wherever the client requires it and wherever there is work overhead.
4.2 Glove selection
The wrong glove is worse than no glove, because it holds the chemical against the skin. Select from the table.

RS-9 solvent | Nitrile, 0.4 mm laminate | About 30 min | Change gloves every 30 minutes of contact; thin nitrile fails in under 10 minutes against hexane
SC-4 descaler | Butyl rubber, 0.7 mm | Over 480 min | Never nitrile; acid penetrates it
Mechanical work, no chemicals | Cut-resistant level C | - | Not for chemical contact
Hot surfaces up to 250 C | Aramid with leather palm | - | Not chemical resistant

[4 Personal protective equipment > 4.2 Glove selection]
Substance or task | Glove material | Breakthrough time | Notes
Handling cleaned seal faces | Lint-free cotton liner | - | Protects the part, not the hand
Table 4.1 - Glove selection. Breakthrough times are from the supplier's permeation data at 23 C.
DANGER RS-9 contains n-hexane. A standard thin nitrile disposable glove gives less than ten minutes of protection against it. For any task with more than incidental contact, use the laminate glove and change it on time.

Work Procedure WP-114
Isolation, lock-out/tag-out and confined space entry
Document number | WP-114
Revision | R5
Issue date | 2025-11-27
Next review | 2027-11-27
Owner | VGM coordinator, Rendell Industrial Services B.V.
Applies to | All Rendell personnel and subcontractors carrying out mechanical or electrical work on client plant
Supersedes | WP-114 R4 of 2024-03-15
Related | RIS-VGM-0042 Safety information and substance register; HX-IOM-400-EN-R7 section 11
THIS PROCEDURE SAVES LIVES Three of the four fatal accidents in Dutch industrial maintenance that the sector body reviewed in its last report involved equipment that was believed to be isolated and was not. Every step in section 5 exists because somebody was killed when it was skipped.

1 Purpose and scope
This procedure sets out how Rendell makes plant safe to work on and how it controls entry into confined spaces. It applies to all work on client plant, in the Rendell workshop, and to subcontractors working under a Rendell order.
Most client sites operate their own permit system. Where they do, that system governs and this procedure describes how Rendell staff work within it. Where a client has no system, or where the work is in the Rendell workshop, this procedure is the system.
THE RULE THAT OVERRIDES EVERYTHING ELSE If you did not isolate it yourself, or you did not see it isolated and prove it dead yourself, it is live. There is no exception to this for experience, for seniority, for time pressure, or for an assurance given over the radio.

2 Definitions
Term | Meaning
Isolation | Positive separation of the equipment from every source of energy, so that the energy cannot be restored accidentally.
Positive isolation | A physical break: a removed spool piece, a spade or blind, or a disconnected and withdrawn electrical circuit. A closed valve alone is not positive isolation.
Lock-out | A personal padlock applied to an isolating device so that it cannot be operated. One lock, one key, one person.
Tag-out | A label on the isolating device stating who applied it, when, and why. A tag warns; it does not prevent.
Stored energy | Energy remaining after isolation: pressure, liquid head, springs, suspended loads, capacitance, heat, chemical reaction.
Proving dead | Testing at the point of work that the energy is actually gone, using a tester that has itself been proved before and after.

[2 Definitions]
Term | Meaning
Confined space | A space that is enclosed or largely enclosed, where there is a foreseeable risk from the atmosphere, from engulfment, or from the difficulty of getting someone out.
Entrant | A person who places any part of their body past the plane of the opening of a confined space.
Standby person | A trained person stationed at the entrance whose only task is the safety of the entrants.
Permit holder | The person in charge of the work covered by a permit, who signs for it and who hands it back.
Permit issuer | The person authorised by the site to issue permits. At a client site this is normally a client employee.
Double block and bleed | Two isolating valves in series with a vent between them that is open to atmosphere, so that any leak past the first valve is visible and relieved.
Table 2.1 - Definitions used in this procedure.

3 Roles
Role | Appointed by | Duties | May not also be
Permit issuer | Site operator | Assesses the isolation, issues and cancels permits, keeps the register | The permit holder for the same permit
Permit holder | Rendell supervisor | Signs for the permit, briefs the team, controls the work, hands the permit back | The standby person
Isolating authority | Site operator | Operates the isolating devices and applies the first lock | -
Entrant | Permit holder | Enters, follows the method, leaves when told | The standby person
Standby person | Permit holder | Keeps the entry log, maintains communication, raises the alarm, never enters | An entrant
Rescue team | Site operator | Trained and equipped retrieval, available within the stated response time | -
Gas tester | Site operator or Rendell, certified | Tests the atmosphere before and during entry | -

[3 Roles]
Table 3.1 - Roles. The last column matters: the standby person has one job and cannot be doing anything else at the same time, including supervising the work.
DANGER The standby person never enters the space, not even to rescue a colleague. Most confined space fatalities are would-be rescuers. If the standby person enters, there is nobody left to raise the alarm and the rescue team arrives to find two casualties instead of one.

4 Energy sources
Before any isolation, list every energy source that can reach the equipment. On a pump installation there are usually more than people expect.
Energy | Typical source on a pump set | Isolation method | How stored energy is released
Electrical | Motor supply, space heater supply, instrument and control supply | Circuit breaker racked out and locked, fuses withdrawn | Prove dead at the terminals; discharge any drive capacitors per the drive manual
Process pressure | Suction and discharge lines | Double block and bleed, or a spade | Vent through the casing vent; confirm the gauge reads zero and crack a joint
Liquid head | Suction vessel above the pump | Close and lock the suction valve; drain the line | Drain to a safe place; remember the volute holds about 4 litres
Seal flush or barrier | Flush line from the discharge or an external pot | Close and lock, or disconnect | Depressurise the barrier pot

[4 Energy sources]
Energy | Typical source on a pump set | Isolation method | How stored energy is released
Thermal | Hot pumped liquid, steam tracing | Isolate the tracing | Allow to cool below 40 C before opening
Mechanical, rotational | Coupling to the motor, a turning gear | Remove the coupling spacer | Make sure the shaft cannot be turned by backflow through the pump
Gravity | A lifted rotor assembly on slings | Set it down on stands | Never work under a suspended load
Chemical | Residue in the casing, reaction with cleaning agents | Flush and purge | Gas test before opening on hazardous service
Pneumatic | Instrument air to control valves | Close and lock the air supply | Bleed the actuator
Nitrogen | Blanketing on a suction vessel | Close and lock | Vent to a safe place; nitrogen asphyxiates without warning
Table 4.1 - Energy sources on a pump set and how each is dealt with.

5 The isolation procedure
Follow these steps in order. Every step is recorded on the isolation certificate in appendix A.
# | Step | What to do | Recorded as
1 | Plan | Identify every energy source using table 4.1. Decide the isolation points and write them on the certificate before touching anything. | Written list
2 | Notify | Tell the control room and anyone affected that the equipment is coming out of service. | Logged
3 | Shut down | Stop the equipment through its normal controls. Do not isolate a running machine. | Confirmed stopped
4 | Isolate | Operate every isolating device identified in step 1. Valves closed, breaker racked out, spades fitted. | Each point ticked
5 | Lock | Apply a personal padlock to every isolating device, or to the lock box holding the keys. One lock per person. | Lock numbers recorded
6 | Tag | Attach a tag to every lock stating name, company, date, time and the work. | Tags fitted

[5 The isolation procedure]
# | Step | What to do | Recorded as
7 | Release stored energy | Vent, drain, discharge, lower, cool. Work down the right-hand column of table 4.1. | Each source ticked
8 | Prove | Test at the point of work that the energy is gone. Prove the tester before and after on a known live source. | Result and tester serial recorded
9 | Try | Attempt to start the equipment through its normal controls, then return the control to off. | Did not start
10 | Sign | The permit holder signs that the isolation is adequate for the work described. | Signature and time
11 | Brief | Brief every person who will work on the equipment on the isolation, the hazards and the limits of the permit. | Names recorded
Table 5.1 - The eleven steps. Steps 8 and 9 are the ones under time pressure that get skipped; they are the two that catch an isolation applied to the wrong machine.

section: 5 The isolation procedure > 5.1 Isolation standard by pressure
text:
[5 The isolation procedure]
5.1 Isolation standard by pressure
The isolation required depends on what the line carries and at what pressure.
Service | Pressure | Minimum isolation | Proving
Water, non-hazardous | Up to 10 bar | One locked valve, vented and drained | Open the vent and confirm no flow
Water, non-hazardous | Above 10 bar | Double block and bleed | Bleed open and confirmed free-flowing to atmosphere
Hot water or condensate above 60 C | Any | Double block and bleed, plus cooling to below 40 C | Temperature measured at the casing
Flammable liquid | Any | Double block and bleed plus a spade, or a removed spool piece | Gas test at the joint before full opening
Toxic or corrosive | Any | Spade or removed spool piece. Valves alone are not accepted. | Gas test and pH check of the drain
Steam | Any | Double block and bleed plus a spade | Confirmed cold and vented
Nitrogen or inert gas | Any | Double block and bleed, vent to a safe place | Oxygen measurement at the opening

section: 5 The isolation procedure > 5.1 Isolation standard by pressure
text:
[5 The isolation procedure > 5.1 Isolation standard by pressure]
Table 5.2 - Isolation standard. Above 10 bar on any service, a single valve is never sufficient.
DANGER A closed valve is not an isolation. Valves pass. A valve that held yesterday may pass today because a piece of scale moved. The bleed between two blocks exists so that a passing first valve shows itself as flow at the bleed instead of as pressure behind the joint you are about to open.

section: 5 The isolation procedure > 5.2 Locks and tags
text:
[5 The isolation procedure]
5.2 Locks and tags
Item | Colour | Used by | Rule
Personal lock | Red | Each individual | One key only, carried by the owner. No master key exists.
Supervisor lock | Blue | Permit holder | Applied first, removed last
Operations lock | Yellow | Site operator | Stays on for the whole outage
Lock box | - | Group lockout | Isolation keys go in, every person puts a personal lock on the box
Out-of-service tag | Yellow and black | Anyone | Marks defective equipment. Not an isolation.
Danger tag | Red and white | Lock owner | Accompanies every personal lock
Table 5.3 - Lock and tag hardware.

[5 The isolation procedure]
5.3 Group lock-out
Where more than two people work on the same isolation, use a lock box. The isolating authority applies the isolations, puts the keys in the box and locks it. Every person working on the equipment then applies their own personal lock to the box. The box cannot be opened until the last personal lock is removed, which means the equipment cannot be re-energised while anybody is still working.

[5 The isolation procedure]
5.4 Shift handover
An isolation that spans a shift change is handed over in person, at the equipment, with the certificate in hand. The outgoing permit holder removes their lock only after the incoming permit holder has applied theirs. A handover by radio or by note is not accepted.

section: 5 The isolation procedure > 5.5 Removing somebody else's lock
text:
[5 The isolation procedure]
5.5 Removing somebody else's lock
A personal lock is removed by its owner. The only exception is the formal lock removal procedure below, used when the owner has left site and cannot return.
# | Step | By
1 | Confirm the owner is genuinely unavailable: phone them. | Permit holder
2 | Physically inspect the equipment and confirm that nobody is working on it and no part is dismantled. | Permit holder plus one witness
3 | Confirm the equipment is safe to re-energise. | Isolating authority
4 | Complete the lock removal form in appendix D, signed by two people. | Permit holder and witness
5 | Obtain the site manager's authorisation. | Site manager
6 | Cut the lock. Record the lock number. | Isolating authority
7 | Inform the lock owner before they next start work. | Permit holder
Table 5.4 - Lock removal in the owner's absence. This has happened four times at Rendell in six years, each time because somebody went home with a key in their pocket.

6 Confined spaces
6.1 What counts
A confined space is not only a tank. The test is whether the space is enclosed enough for the atmosphere to go wrong, or for a person to be hard to get out. The following are treated as confined spaces at Rendell:
• Process vessels, tanks, silos and columns.
• Pump pits and sumps deeper than 1.2 metres.
• Valve chambers and inspection pits.
• Culverts, sewers and interceptors.
• Large bore pipework a person can enter.
• Heat exchanger shells and water boxes.
• Trenches deeper than 1.2 metres where gas may collect.
• The inside of a drained cooling tower basin with the fan stopped.
• Any space the client has designated as a confined space.
A space becomes confined because of what is happening in it, not only because of its shape. An open-topped pit is confined while solvent cleaning is going on inside it, even though it is open to the sky.

[6 Confined spaces]
6.2 Avoiding entry
The first question on every entry permit is whether the work can be done without going in. Camera inspection, extraction from outside, long-handled tools and removing the item to the workshop all avoid the entry altogether, and each has solved a job at Rendell that was first planned as an entry.

[6 Confined spaces]
6.3 Atmospheric testing
Test before entry, from outside, at three depths: near the opening, at mid-depth and near the bottom. Heavy vapours collect low, which is exactly where somebody will be working.
Measurement | Acceptable | Action if outside | Instrument
Oxygen | 19.5 to 23.5 per cent by volume | Do not enter. Ventilate and re-test. | Electrochemical cell, bump tested that day
Flammable gas or vapour | Below 10 per cent of the lower explosive limit | Do not enter. Ventilate, find the source, re-test. | Catalytic bead or infrared
Hydrogen sulphide | Below 5 ppm | Do not enter. Air-fed equipment and a fresh assessment. | Electrochemical cell
Carbon monoxide | Below 20 ppm | Do not enter. Ventilate and find the source. | Electrochemical cell
Solvent vapour where RS-9 has been used | Below the 8-hour limit of 200 ppm | Ventilate. Air-fed equipment if work must continue. | Photo-ionisation detector

[6 Confined spaces > 6.3 Atmospheric testing]
Table 6.1 - Atmospheric acceptance criteria. All four of the first readings must be in range at all three depths before entry is permitted.
DANGER Oxygen above 23.5 per cent is as dangerous as oxygen below 19.5 per cent. An oxygen-enriched atmosphere makes clothing and hair burn fiercely from a spark that would otherwise do nothing. Enrichment usually means a leaking oxygen hose left in the space overnight.
Testing continues during the entry. Where a detector is worn by the entrants it runs continuously; otherwise the standby person tests at the opening at least every 30 minutes and records the result on the entry log. Any reading outside the range in table 6.1 means immediate evacuation, not an investigation.

[6 Confined spaces]
6.4 Ventilation
Situation | Ventilation | Note
Clean, water-only service, no work generating fumes | Natural ventilation with both openings clear | Confirm there are two openings
Any solvent or paint use | Forced extraction from the lowest point | Vapour is heavier than air
Welding or hot work | Forced extraction plus local fume extraction at the arc | Separate hot work permit required
After acid cleaning | Forced ventilation for at least 30 minutes before entry, then re-test | Hydrogen may have accumulated
Nitrogen blanketed vessel | Forced ventilation with a full air change count, then re-test | Never rely on time alone
Table 6.2 - Ventilation requirements.
DANGER Never ventilate a confined space with oxygen. People have done it, believing it would help, and have set the space alight.

[6 Confined spaces]
6.5 Entry controls
Control | Requirement
Entry permit | Issued before entry, held at the entrance by the standby person
Standby person | Present and dedicated for the whole of the entry, with no other duties
Communication | Continuous voice or line-of-sight contact; a check every two minutes where contact is by radio
Entry log | Every entrant signed in and out by name and time, kept by the standby person
Retrieval equipment | Harness and line rigged to a tripod or davit for any vertical entry deeper than 1.5 metres
Rescue arrangement | A trained and equipped team able to begin retrieval within 6 minutes of the alarm, confirmed before entry
Lighting | 24 volt or lower, or intrinsically safe, in any wet or flammable space
Electrical tools | 24 volt, or air driven, or battery. 230 volt tools are not taken into a confined space.
Gas detector | Bump tested the same day, calibration within date, carried by an entrant where continuous monitoring is required

[6 Confined spaces > 6.5 Entry controls]
Control | Requirement
Escape set | Carried where the atmosphere could deteriorate faster than the entrants can get out
Table 6.3 - Entry controls.
6.6 Stopping an entry
The entry stops and everybody comes out immediately if any of the following happens. There is no assessment to make and no permission to seek.
• Any gas reading moves outside the limits of table 6.1.
• A gas detector alarms, whatever the reading afterwards.
• Communication with the standby person is lost.
• Ventilation stops.
• Lighting fails.
• An entrant feels unwell, dizzy, or reports a headache.
• The site alarm sounds.
• The permit expires and has not been extended.
• Anybody, inside or outside, calls for evacuation.

7 Permits
7.1 Validity
Permit | Maximum validity | Extension | Re-test required
Isolation certificate | Until cancelled | - | On any change to the isolation
Work permit, general | 8 hours | Once, by 4 hours, by the issuer in person | No
Confined space entry permit | 8 hours | Once, by 4 hours, by the issuer in person | Yes, full atmospheric re-test before the extension
Hot work permit | 4 hours | Once, by 2 hours | Yes, flammable gas re-test
Excavation permit | 7 days | By the issuer | No
Table 7.1 - Permit validity. A permit that has expired is dead: the work stops, the space is cleared and a new permit is raised. A permit is never extended retrospectively.
A permit is cancelled and handed back when the work is finished, when the shift ends, when the permit expires, or at any break longer than one hour. Handing the permit back is a positive act: the permit holder goes to the issuer, confirms the state of the plant and signs.

[7 Permits]
7.2 Returning to service
# | Step | By
1 | Confirm the work is complete and tested. | Permit holder
2 | Account for every tool, part and person. | Permit holder
3 | Refit guards, covers and insulation. | Fitter
4 | Close drains and vents, refit plugs with new washers. | Fitter
5 | Hand the permit back and sign it off. | Permit holder
6 | Each person removes their own personal lock. | Each person
7 | Remove the supervisor lock. | Permit holder
8 | Remove the operations lock and the isolation. | Isolating authority
9 | Confirm with the control room before re-energising. | Isolating authority
10 | Stand clear and start. Watch the first two minutes. | Operator
Table 7.2 - Returning to service. Step 2 is not a formality: a spanner left inside a pump casing has written off an impeller twice in the last five years.

section: 8 Worked example: changing a mechanical seal on an HX-400
text:
8 Worked example: changing a mechanical seal on an HX-400
This example shows the procedure applied to the most common job Rendell does. The pump is on a cooling water duty at 7 bar and 45 C, suction from a vessel 6 metres above the pump.
# | Action | Why
1 | Raise the isolation certificate listing: motor supply, space heater supply, suction valve, discharge valve, seal flush line, instrument air to the recirculation valve. | Six sources, not one. The space heater supply is the one people forget.
2 | Ask the control room to stop the pump and put the standby pump in service. | The duty must be covered first
3 | Rack out and lock the motor breaker. Lock the heater supply. | Electrical isolation
4 | Close and lock the discharge valve. | Prevents backflow through the non-return valve turning the pump
5 | Close and lock the suction valve. | Stops the 6 metre head from the vessel
6 | Close and lock the seal flush. | The flush comes off the discharge of the running standby pump

Question | Answer

10 Worked example: entering a pump pit
Pump P-1408B sits in a concrete pit 2.6 metres deep with a single access hatch. The pump handles condensate at 95 C. The job is to replace the coupling element.
# | Action | Why it matters here
1 | Ask whether the entry can be avoided. | It cannot: the coupling is inside the pit. Record that the question was asked.
2 | Raise the isolation certificate for the pump. | Six energy sources as in table 8.1, plus the steam tracing on the condensate line.
3 | Let the pump and the line cool below 40 C. | 95 C condensate. Cooling takes several hours; plan for it rather than rushing it.
4 | Raise the confined space entry permit. | The pit is deeper than 1.2 metres and has one way out.

# | Action | Why it matters here
5 | Test the atmosphere from outside at three depths. | Condensate leaks raise humidity and can displace oxygen at the bottom; steam has been known to strip the oxygen reading.

section: 11 Worked example: an isolation that went wrong
text:
11 Worked example: an isolation that went wrong
The following happened at a client site in 2023. Nobody was injured. It is reproduced here because every one of the contributing factors is ordinary.
What happened | What should have happened
A fitter was sent to change a seal on 'the duty cooling water pump'. Two identical pumps stood side by side, tagged P-1203A and P-1203B, with the tag plates weathered and hard to read. | The work order names the tag. The fitter confirms the tag at the machine before starting, not from the layout drawing.
The control room isolated P-1203A electrically. The fitter began work on P-1203B, which was the standby and was not running at that moment. | The fitter applies their own lock and proves dead at the machine they are going to work on. Proving dead at the right machine would have found this at once.

section: 11 Worked example: an isolation that went wrong
text:
[11 Worked example: an isolation that went wrong]
What happened | What should have happened
The fitter removed the coupling guard and the spacer. The machine was still live and the standby start logic was active. | Steps 8 and 9 of table 5.1: prove dead, then try to start. Neither was done.
The duty pump tripped on a process upset. The standby start logic called P-1203B. The motor started with the coupling spacer removed and the guard off. | With the breaker racked out and locked, the start command would have done nothing.
The fitter was bent over the bearing housing, not in line with the shaft, and was not hurt. | -
Table 11.1 - The 2023 near miss. Four separate barriers were available; none was used, because each one felt unnecessary given the one before.

section: 11 Worked example: an isolation that went wrong
text:
[11 Worked example: an isolation that went wrong]
THE LESSON Nobody in this story was careless or untrained. The fitter was experienced and had done the job dozens of times. What was missing was the habit of proving dead at the machine, every time, including when it is obviously already off.
12 Gas detector management
Activity | Who | Frequency | Record
Bump test with span gas | User | Before each day's use | Instrument log and the permit
Full calibration | Workshop or supplier | Every 6 months | Calibration certificate
Sensor replacement | Supplier | Oxygen every 2 years, toxic every 3 years, catalytic on failure | Service record
Battery and alarm check | User | Before each use | Instrument log
Post-incident check | Workshop | After any alarm, drop or exposure to silicone or solvent | Service record
Zero in clean air | User | Before each use, outdoors | Instrument log

[12 Gas detector management]
Table 12.1 - Detector management. A catalytic bead sensor can be poisoned by silicone or by high solvent vapour and will then under-read without any fault indication. That is why the bump test is daily and not monthly.

Onderhoudsvoorschrift OV-220
Preventief onderhoud aan pompinstallaties
Documentnummer | OV-220
Revisie | R4
Uitgiftedatum | 2026-02-14
Volgende herziening | 2028-02-14
Eigenaar | Afdeling Onderhoud, Rendell Industrial Services B.V.
Toepassingsgebied | Alle centrifugaalpompinstallaties van de HX-serie in beheer bij Rendell
Vervangt | OV-220 R3 van 2024-05-06
Samenhangende documenten | HX-IOM-400-EN-R7 (fabrikantenhandleiding), WP-114 (veiligstellen en besloten ruimten), RIS-VGM-0042 (stoffenregister)
Dit voorschrift beschrijft wat er aan een pompinstallatie gebeurt, hoe vaak, en waaraan het resultaat moet voldoen. Waar dit voorschrift en de handleiding van de fabrikant van elkaar afwijken, geldt het strengste van de twee.

1 Doel en toepassingsgebied
Dit voorschrift legt het preventieve onderhoud aan pompinstallaties vast. Het doel is drieledig: de installaties beschikbaar houden, de kosten van storingen beperken, en kunnen aantonen dat het onderhoud is uitgevoerd zoals de fabrikant en de wetgever dat verlangen.
Het voorschrift geldt voor alle pompinstallaties van de HX-serie die Rendell in beheer heeft, zowel op eigen locatie als bij opdrachtgevers waar Rendell het onderhoud contractueel verzorgt. Voor pompen van een ander merk geldt OV-221.
Correctief onderhoud, dus herstel na een storing, valt buiten dit voorschrift en is beschreven in OV-230.

2 Definities en afkortingen
Term | Betekenis
Preventief onderhoud | Onderhoud dat op vaste intervallen wordt uitgevoerd, ongeacht de toestand van de installatie.
Toestandsafhankelijk onderhoud | Onderhoud dat wordt uitgevoerd op grond van een gemeten toestand, bijvoorbeeld trilling of olieanalyse.
Correctief onderhoud | Herstel na een storing of een geconstateerde afwijking.
Draaiuren | Het aantal uren dat de pomp daadwerkelijk heeft gedraaid, afgelezen van de urenteller in de besturing.
Kritikaliteit | Klasse A, B of C. Zie paragraaf 5.2.
Nulmeting | De meting die bij inbedrijfstelling of na een revisie is vastgelegd en waarmee latere metingen worden vergeleken.
BEP | Best efficiency point, het punt van hoogste rendement op de pompkarakteristiek.
TIR | Total indicated runout, de totale uitslag van een meetklok over een hele omwenteling.
Maximo | Het onderhoudsbeheersysteem waarin alle werkorders en meetwaarden worden vastgelegd.

[2 Definities en afkortingen]
Term | Betekenis
Veiligstellen | Het geheel van maatregelen uit WP-114 waarmee een installatie veilig te bewerken wordt gemaakt.
Tabel 2.1 - Definities.
3 Verantwoordelijkheden
Rol | Verantwoordelijk voor
Onderhoudsmanager | Vaststellen van dit voorschrift, toewijzen van middelen, goedkeuren van uitstel van klasse A-taken.
Werkvoorbereider | Plannen van de werkorders, beschikbaar stellen van onderdelen, taakkaarten en vergunningen.
Uitvoerend monteur | Uitvoeren van de taakkaart, vastleggen van meetwaarden, melden van afwijkingen dezelfde dag.
Operator | De wekelijkse ronde, directe melding van bijzonderheden.
Specialist conditiebewaking | Trillingsmetingen, interpretatie en advies over vervroegd ingrijpen.
VGM-coordinator | Toezicht op veilig werken, zie WP-114 en RIS-VGM-0042.
Tabel 3.1 - Verantwoordelijkheden.

4 Onderhoudsstrategie
De strategie per installatie volgt uit de kritikaliteit. Hoe hoger de kritikaliteit, hoe meer er gemeten wordt en hoe korter de intervallen.
Kritikaliteit | Omschrijving | Strategie | Reservepomp
A | Uitval leidt tot productiestilstand, milieuschade of onveilige situatie | Preventief volgens dit voorschrift plus toestandsafhankelijk: trilling per kwartaal, olieanalyse per kwartaal | Geinstalleerde reservepomp vereist
B | Uitval leidt tot verminderde capaciteit of extra kosten | Preventief volgens dit voorschrift, trilling per kwartaal | Reserve-aggregaat op voorraad
C | Uitval heeft beperkte gevolgen | Preventief op verlengde intervallen, geen vaste trillingsmeting | Niet vereist
Tabel 4.1 - Strategie per kritikaliteitsklasse.
Voor klasse C-installaties mogen de intervallen in tabel 6.1 met een factor 1,5 worden verlengd, met uitzondering van de olieverversing: die blijft gebonden aan draaiuren en kalendertijd.

5.1 Codering
Elke pompinstallatie heeft een tagnummer volgens het patroon P-XXYYZ, waarbij XX het gebouwnummer is, YY het volgnummer binnen het gebouw en Z de letter A of B voor een pompenpaar.

Tabel 6.2 - Toegestane afwijking van de planning.
LET OP De olieverversing kent geen tolerantie op de draaiuren. Bij 4.000 draaiuren of 12 maanden, wat zich het eerst voordoet, wordt de olie ververst. Dit is de meest overgeslagen taak in het hele voorschrift en de meest voorkomende oorzaak van voortijdige lagerschade.

7 Smering
7.1 Oliesoort
Alle HX-pompen worden gesmeerd met Halstrom HLP-46, een minerale olie van de viscositeitsklasse ISO VG 46. Er wordt geen andere soort gebruikt en soorten worden niet gemengd. Is de aanwezige soort onbekend, dan wordt afgetapt, gespoeld en opnieuw gevuld.

[7 Smering]
7.2 Verversingsschema
Gelegenheid | Interval | Opmerking
Inloopverversing | Na 300 draaiuren | Na inbedrijfstelling en opnieuw na elke revisie. Ongeacht het uiterlijk van de olie.
Reguliere verversing | Elke 4.000 draaiuren of 12 maanden | Wat zich het eerst voordoet
Vervroegd, op uiterlijk | Direct | Melkwitte olie (water), donkere olie (oververhitting), zichtbare deeltjes
Vervroegd, op analyse | Direct | Watergehalte boven 500 ppm of zuurgetal boven 1,5 mg KOH/g
Na een storing met lagerschade | Direct | Samen met de lagervervanging
Motorlagers vetten | Elke 2.000 draaiuren | Met Halstrom LGHP-2. De pomplagers worden nooit gevet.
Tabel 7.2 - Wanneer de olie wordt ververst.
WAARSCHUWING Het lagerhuis van de pomp heeft geen smeernippel. Wie er een zoekt, staat bij de verkeerde machine. Vet in het lagerhuis van de pomp leidt tot zekere lagerschade.

8 Conditiebewaking
8.1 Trillingsmeting
Bij kritikaliteit A en B wordt per kwartaal gemeten op beide lagerhuizen, in drie richtingen: horizontaal, verticaal en axiaal. De totaalwaarde in mm/s effectief wordt getrend; daarnaast wordt een spectrum opgeslagen zodat een stijging kan worden verklaard.
Grenswaarde | Waarde | Actie
Nulmeting | Vastgelegd bij inbedrijfstelling | Referentie voor alle latere metingen
Aandachtswaarde | 2,8 mm/s | Meetfrequentie verhogen naar maandelijks
Alarmwaarde | 4.5 mm/s | Oorzaak onderzoeken binnen twee weken, spectrum analyseren
Afschakelwaarde | 7.1 mm/s | Pomp uit bedrijf nemen, reservepomp inschakelen, onderzoek voor herstart
Stapverandering | Toename van meer dan 1,5 mm/s tussen twee metingen | Direct onderzoeken, ook onder de alarmwaarde
Tabel 8.1 - Grenswaarden trilling, totaalwaarde effectief (RMS), gemeten op het lagerhuis.
Frequentie | Waarschijnlijke oorzaak | Vervolgactie

[8 Conditiebewaking > 8.1 Trillingsmeting]

1x toerental | Onbalans | Waaier controleren op aanslag of erosie; balanceren bij revisie
2x toerental | Uitlijnfout | Uitlijning controleren, leidingspanning uitsluiten
5x toerental (schoeppassage) | Hydraulisch, te krappe spleet bij de tong | Bedrijfspunt toetsen aan het werkgebied
0,4 tot 0,48x toerental | Oliewerveling in het lager | Oliesoort en oliepeil controleren

8.2 Olieanalyse
Kenmerk | Nieuw | Grens | Betekenis bij overschrijding

Tabel 8.3 - Grenswaarden olieanalyse. Monsters worden genomen bij draaiende pomp of direct na stilstand, nooit uit de afgetapte olie.

9 Uitlijning
Uitlijning wordt halfjaarlijks koud gecontroleerd, en daarnaast altijd na werkzaamheden waarbij de pomp, de motor of de leidingen zijn losgenomen. Uitlijnen voordat de leidingen zijn aangesloten heeft geen waarde.
Grootheid | Koude grenswaarde | Warme controle | Methode
Parallelle verplaatsing | 0.08 mm | 0,12 mm | Laser of meetklok
Hoekafwijking | 0.06 mm per 100 mm | 0,10 mm per 100 mm | Laser of meetklok
Koppelingsafstand | 4,0 mm +/- 0,5 | gelijk aan koud | Voelermaat op vier punten
Zachte voet | 0,05 mm | - | Meetklok, bout voor bout
Leidingspanning | 0,05 mm verplaatsing bij losnemen | - | Meetklok op de koppeling
Tabel 9.1 - Uitlijntoleranties, gelijk aan tabel 5.6 van de fabrikantenhandleiding.
Bij media warmer dan 80 C groeit de pomp ten opzichte van de motor. De koude uitlijning wordt dan met de verwachte groei voorgecompenseerd: bij water van 120 C stijgt de hartlijn van de pomp ongeveer 0,09 mm.

10 Asafdichtingen
De standaardafdichting is de cartridge MS-28 enkelwerkende cartridge-seal, onderdeelnummer HX-4-SEAL-28S. De afdichting wordt als geheel vervangen en in het veld niet geopend. De verwachte levensduur is 16.000 draaiuren in schoon water tot 60 C.
Verschijnsel | Waarschijnlijke oorzaak | Actie
Lekkage direct na montage | Stelklemmen niet verwijderd | Klemmen verwijderen; zie IOM paragraaf 9.6 stap 12
Lekkage direct na montage | O-ring beschadigd bij montage | Cartridge vervangen, smeren met het verpompte medium
Lekkage na enkele weken | Drooglopen | Spoeling en droogloopbeveiliging controleren
Lekkage na enkele maanden | Abrasieve deeltjes in het medium | Dubbelwerkende afdichting met spervloeistof overwegen
Terugkerende lekkage op dezelfde pomp | Leidingspanning vervormt het huis | Leidingondersteuning aanpassen, zie paragraaf 9
Terugkerende lekkage op dezelfde pomp | Bedrijfspunt ver van het BEP | Bedrijfsvoering aanpassen; minimaal 15% van het BEP-debiet

[10 Asafdichtingen]
Tabel 10.1 - Afdichtingsproblemen. Een afdichting die herhaald faalt is bijna nooit een afdichtingsprobleem.

Tabel 11.1 - Conservering.

[11 Reservepompen en conservering]
WAARSCHUWING Achtergebleven vloeistof in het spiraalhuis bevriest en scheurt een gietijzeren huis. Na het openen van de aftapplug blijft ongeveer 4 liter in het huis van een HX-400 achter; die moet er bij vorstgevaar met perslucht uit.

13 Registratie en prestatie-indicatoren
Elke uitgevoerde taak wordt dezelfde dag in Maximo afgemeld, met de gemeten waarden en de bestede tijd. Een taak die niet is afgemeld, geldt als niet uitgevoerd.

Aandeel preventief | Preventieve uren gedeeld door het totaal aan onderhoudsuren | Minimaal 70%
Terugkerende storingen | Aantal storingen op dezelfde tag binnen twaalf maanden | Maximaal 1
Gemiddelde tijd tussen storingen | Draaiuren gedeeld door het aantal storingen, per klasse | Klasse A minimaal 12.000 uur
Volledigheid meetwaarden | Aandeel afgemelde werkorders met alle verplichte meetwaarden ingevuld | Minimaal 98%
Uitstel klasse A | Aantal uitgestelde klasse A-taken per kwartaal | Nul
Tabel 13.1 - Prestatie-indicatoren, per kwartaal gerapporteerd aan de onderhoudsmanager.

[17 Storingsanalyse]
Tabel 17.1 - Storingen over drie jaar, 122 meldingen in totaal. Asafdichtingen en lagers samen zijn goed voor meer dan de helft; beide zijn te beinvloeden met onderhoud dat al in dit voorschrift staat.
De conclusie van de analyse over 2025 was dat het voorschrift inhoudelijk klopt maar dat de naleving tekortschiet. Van de negentien lagerschades waren er veertien aan een pomp waarvan de olieverversing meer dan duizend draaiuren te laat was. Daarom is in revisie R4 de tolerantie op de olieverversing geschrapt.

18 Werkwijze bij een storing tijdens preventief onderhoud
Wordt tijdens een preventieve taak een afwijking gevonden, dan geldt het volgende. Het doel is dat de monteur niet zelf hoeft te beslissen of iets erg genoeg is om te melden.

Trilling boven afschakelwaarde | Reservepomp inschakelen, pomp stoppen | Directe melding aan de werkvoorbereider | Ja

19 Overdracht aan de opdrachtgever
Werkt Rendell op locatie van een opdrachtgever, dan gelden aanvullend de volgende afspraken.
Onderwerp | Afspraak
Werkvergunning | Altijd van de opdrachtgever, volgens diens systeem. WP-114 beschrijft hoe Rendell daarbinnen werkt.
Registratie | In het systeem van de opdrachtgever, en een kopie in Maximo.
Afwijkingen | Dezelfde dag gemeld aan de contactpersoon van de opdrachtgever, schriftelijk.
Reserveonderdelen | Eigendom van de opdrachtgever tenzij anders overeengekomen; voorraad conform tabel 12.1.
Afgetapte olie en afval | Via de afvalstroom van de opdrachtgever, met weegbon.
Stoffen meegebracht door Rendell | Alleen stoffen uit RIS-VGM-0042, vooraf gemeld bij de opdrachtgever.
Rapportage | Per kwartaal: uitgevoerde taken, afwijkingen, trillingstrends en advies.
